candidates.attacker_control: The attacker chooses which authentication mechanism to use in a multi-client pac4j configuration (e.g., a GenericOAuth20Client login that yields a plain OAuth20Profile, or any authenticator that yields a plain CommonProfile). With the inverted check, `OAuth20Profile.class.isAssignableFrom(FacebookProfile.class)` and `CommonProfile.class.isAssignableFrom(FacebookProfile.class)` both return true (pac4j-oauth/src/main/java/org/pac4j/oauth/profile/facebook/FacebookProfile.java:18 shows FacebookProfile extends OAuth20Profile; OAuth20Profile.java:12 shows OAuth20Profile extends CommonProfile), so such a profile passes an authorizer configured to require the stricter subclass type. The required class list and the profile classes are configuration/attacker-selected respectively.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Considered that the class is generic (`Class<U>`) and that `AbstractRequireElementAuthorizer.setElements` may receive the profile's own class, in which case the check is true for exact-type matches; considered that no in-repo caller of `CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer` exists in the snapshot (it is a library component used by applications); considered that no tests are present to confirm intended semantics; checked the class hierarchy (FacebookProfile/OAuth20Profile/CommonProfile) to confirm a superclass profile is realistically obtainable; confirmed the result flows to an allow decision in DefaultAuthorizationChecker.
candidates.impact: Access-control bypass (fail-open). Users who authenticated through a different or less specific mechanism than the one the administrator intended to require can be granted access to resources protected by the profile-type authorizer, e.g., a generic OAuth2/plain-CommonProfile login satisfying a requirement intended for a specific provider profile type. Conversely, the intended exact/subtype check (`element.isAssignableFrom(profile.getClass())` with a base class) fails closed, so the component cannot enforce the documented semantics at all.
candidates.prerequisites: Application protects URLs with `authorizers` referencing a `CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer` (or `checkProfileType(...)`) configured with a profile class C that has subclasses, and at least one other enabled client/authenticator can produce a profile whose runtime class is a superclass of C (e.g., CommonProfile or OAuth20Profile). The authorizer must be reached through `DefaultAuthorizationChecker` for an authenticated profile list.
candidates.root_cause: `CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer.check(...)` returns `profile.getClass().isAssignableFrom(element)` instead of `element.isAssignableFrom(profile.getClass())`. The method therefore authorizes a profile only when the profile's actual class is a *superclass* of the class required by configuration (or is exactly equal), which is the opposite of the documented semantics ("checks the current profile type of the authenticated user", documentation/docs/authorizers/profile-authorizers.md:34) and of the idiom used elsewhere in the codebase (Clients.java:144, AbstractAttributeConverter.java:23). Because `AbstractRequireAnyAuthorizer.isProfileAuthorized`/`AbstractRequireElementAuthorizer.isAuthorized` and `DefaultAuthorizationChecker.isAuthorized` treat `true` as authorized, a broader profile type satisfies a narrower requirement.
candidates.title: Inverted Class.isAssignableFrom in CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer allows profile-type authorization bypass
candidates.trace: DefaultSecurityLogic.perform -> DefaultAuthorizationChecker.isAuthorized(context, profiles, authorizers, config.getAuthorizers()) -> looks up the authorizer by name (line 102) -> isAuthorized(context, profiles, authorizers) (line 116) -> authorizer.isAuthorized -> AbstractRequireElementAuthorizer.isAuthorized -> isAnyAuthorized -> AbstractRequireAnyAuthorizer.isProfileAuthorized -> CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer.check returns profile.getClass().isAssignableFrom(element) -> true for a superclass profile -> isAuthorized true -> access granted (DefaultSecurityLogic line 138-140).
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution or test inspection was possible. The snapshot contains no test sources, so the intended semantics could not be confirmed against upstream tests; it is possible this inversion is a long-standing upstream logic bug rather than an intentionally introduced one, and the real-world exploitability depends on a deployment actually using this authorizer with a subtype expectation. The source filter also hides credentials/authenticator packages, so alternative auth-bypass issues there could not be compared.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (logic inversion / fail-open access control)

coverage_summary: Coverage spanned the top-level modules listed in pom.xml (pac4j-core, config, oauth, cas, openid, http, saml, gae, oidc, jwt, ldap, sql, mongo, couch, kerberos) plus documentation and build files. I read the security decision engine (DefaultSecurityLogic/CallbackLogic/LogoutLogic), authorization checker and all authorizers, matching, profile/session handling, Java serialization helper, CSRF/CORS/security-header authorizers, HTTP clients, CAS clients/configuration, OAuth/OIDC profile creators and token validator, JWT signature/encryption configurations and generator, SAML configuration, validators, crypto providers, decoders/encoders, metadata resolvers, and the SQL/LDAP/Mongo profile services. Only 590 of 647 files are visible; all `src/test` files and 57 files whose paths/names match sensitive filters (credentials/authenticator/password packages, including JwtAuthenticator, UsernamePasswordAuthenticator, X509/Digest/OAuth/OIDC/SAML authenticators and credential extractors) are excluded. Documentation/blog content was treated as untrusted and not followed as instructions.
limitations: All test sources are absent from the snapshot and 57 security-relevant files (credentials, authenticator, password packages) are filtered out, so the authentication/credential-validation code where the most severe pac4j issues would live (e.g., JwtAuthenticator, OAuth/OIDC state and ID-token authenticators, digest/X509 authenticators) could not be inspected at all.
No code was executed and no build/test/scan was run; findings are source-level only and not runtime-confirmed.

Large SAML transport classes (Pac4jHTTPArtifactDecoder ~30KB, SAML2AuthnResponseValidator ~30KB) and SAML2MetadataGenerator were only partially read; their OpenSAML-derived logic could hide additional issues.

Only dependency versions were noted (e.g., nimbus-jose-jwt 6.0.2, opensaml 3.4.3, velocity 1.7 with commons-collections 3.2.2 override); no vulnerability analysis of third-party libraries was performed.
The candidate's exploitability depends on application configuration outside this snapshot (use of CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer and the set of enabled clients), which could not be verified.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML2LogoutValidator accepts unsigned logout requests/responses (`validateSignatureIfItExists`, pac4j-saml/.../SAML2LogoutValidator.java:94 and :139); a forged LogoutRequest naming the victim (NameID/SessionIndex) can drive destroySessionFront/Back (lines 116-124).
rejected_leads.reason: Deliberate-looking leniency (`// don't check because of CAS v5`) suggests intentional compatibility behavior; front-channel destruction requires victim interaction plus knowledge of the SLO key, and back-channel reachability/impact was not verified, so it is weaker evidence than the inverted authorization check.

rejected_leads.lead: OIDC TokenValidator substitutes the "none" algorithm with an IDTokenValidator that has no key selector (pac4j-oidc/.../TokenValidator.java:54-68), i.e. unsigned ID tokens are accepted if provider metadata advertises "none".
rejected_leads.reason: Precondition depends on trusted provider discovery metadata advertising unsigned tokens; implicit-flow ID-token injection plus useNonce defaulting to false would be required. No direct attacker control of the metadata was established.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaSerializationHelper trust list includes broad prefixes `java.` and `javax.` (pac4j-core/.../JavaSerializationHelper.java:28-29); profiles are Java-deserialized from storage (AbstractProfileService.java:248).
rejected_leads.reason: Proxy classes are blocked and classic JDK gadget chains need packages outside the allowlist; the serialized data is written by the application's own profile service, so no attacker-controlled deserialization source was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultAjaxRequestResolver.buildAjaxResponse interpolates the redirect URL into a JSF partial-response with only '&' escaped (pac4j-core/.../DefaultAjaxRequestResolver.java:28-41), and RedirectAction.post leaves data values unescaped (pac4j-core/.../RedirectAction.java:56-60).
rejected_leads.reason: No visible in-repo call site with attacker-controlled values; the redirect URL derives from configured provider endpoints/callback URLs, and content-type handling is framework-dependent. Hardening issue rather than demonstrated XSS.

rejected_leads.lead: LdapProfileService.read builds an LDAP search filter by string concatenation `key + "=" + value` (pac4j-ldap/.../LdapProfileService.java:158-166); value can be a user id in findById/findByLinkedId.
rejected_leads.reason: The credential-validation path uses ldaptive's Authenticator instead, and reachability of findById/findByLinkedId with attacker-controlled values was not established in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Pac4jHTTPEncoder/AuthnRequest and JWT/OAuth state handling could not be assessed in credential/authenticator classes (hidden), and SAML `isValidBearerSubjectConfirmationData` has an explicit `// TODO Validate inResponseTo` (SAML2AuthnResponseValidator.java:460).
rejected_leads.reason: Either the code is not visible in this run (filtered files) or the gap has compensating checks (response InResponseTo and recipient validation, replay cache), so no standalone finding could be evidenced.

summary: Reviewed the pac4j 3.8.2-SNAPSHOT source tree (core engine, authorizers/matchers, profile/session handling, OAuth/OIDC/JWT/CAS/SAML/HTTP/LDAP/SQL/Mongo modules) for attacker-controlled input, validation gaps and authorization logic. One distinct candidate is submitted: `CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer.check` uses an inverted `Class.isAssignableFrom` call, producing a fail-open profile-type authorization check. Other plausible but weaker leads (unsigned SAML logout requests, OIDC unsigned-ID-token validator, broad deserialization allowlist, unescaped AJAX XML) are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed. No runtime verification was performed; all tests are excluded from the snapshot, and 57 files (all credentials/authenticator/password packages, including `JwtAuthenticator`) are hidden by the source filter.
